newsitem.title: USA: Miami tourist officials relieved Cunanan case ends.
newsitem.headline: Miami tourist officials relieved Cunanan case ends.

text.p: Among those most relieved on Thursday by the end of the manhunt for Gianni Versace's killer may have been the leaders of Miami's multi-billion-dollar tourism industry.

The July 15 slaying of the world-famous fashion designer in front of his home in the heart of Miami Beach's tourist district was a blow to a region that promotes itself as a visitor's paradise, but seems constantly to be fighting off the effects of its stubbornly high violent crime rate.
"This is a great relief for the city of Miami Beach. We're accustomed to greeting tourists, not searching out killers," Miami Beach Mayor Seymour Gelber told Reuters in an interview.

"The likes of Sylvester Stallone and Madonna are the visitors we usually welcome. And my job in great part is to hand out keys to the city and make proclamations and point out to the world that the sun is shining here," he said.
"The last 10 days have been rather dreary."

An intense nationwide search for Andrew Cunanan, believed responsible for Versace's death, ended before dawn on Thursday, when police confirmed that a man found dead after barricading himself on a houseboat was the alleged serial killer.
Versace's slaying reminded visitors, and the businesses that rely upon them, of the 12-month period five years ago when nine European tourists were murdered in Florida.
"Miami has such a bad reputation in Germany. This is very, very bad," Britt Steinhardt, a German flight attendant, said in the wake of the killing.

Versace's death was followed by 10 days in which uniformed police, FBI agents and other authorities searching for a man described as "armed and dangerous" mingled with Miami Beach's sunbathers and rollerbladers.

Reminders of the killing were everywhere. News crews camped out in front of police headquarters. A heap of flowers and other memorials to the designer grew in front of Versace's mansion. And Cunanan's "Most Wanted" poster was ubiquitous on shop doors and nightclub walls.

To the added chagrin of tourist officials, news reports in Italy, the designer's home, and France, a centre of the world's fashion industry, in particular linked the designer's death to the earlier tourist killings and even race rioting in the city in the early 1980s.

"I think everyone can feel relieved that law enforcement was able to find him," said Mayco Villafana, communications director for the Greater Miami Convention and Visitors Bureau, after police confirmed they had found Cunanan dead.

"For us, in the visitor industry, it's time again to reinforce how unique and individual this case was," he said. "It really could have occured anywhere (and) we hope that this doesn't have any lingering effect on our community as a tourist mecca."

Miami and Miami Beach are technically separate cities, a point that Miami Beach officials have been anxious to make during Miami's recent corruption scandals. But in the eyes of tourists, visitors and most residents, the two cities are one.

Tourists spent a record $10.9 billion in greater Miami last year, indicating that the industry had rebounded from a 1994 downturn that followed the string of tourist attacks. And for the first quarter of 1997, tourists pumped another $3.4 billion into the local economy, another record.
Villafana said the tourist office was working to restore any luster lost because of Versace's death.

"Every indication that we've had so far is that 1997 is a very good year and perhaps could be another banner year for the industry," he said. "Certainly when you have these kinds of incidents that are not tourism related, however, they do affect your community and your product."
